newsitem.title: UK: Briton lands Nobel for flash of inspiration.
newsitem.headline: Briton lands Nobel for flash of inspiration.

text.p: British professor James Mirrlees, whose great flash of academic inspiration came almost 30 years ago, won the Nobel Economics prize on Tuesday for his work on how tax levels can motivate people.
The 60-year-old Scotsman, who lists "reading detective stories and other forms of mathematics" among his hobbies, shared the prize with Canadian William Vickrey.
Mirrlees, bombarded with congratulations by fellow "dons" at Cambridge University, said he first thought the telephone call from Sweden telling him of his prize was a hoax.
"It was extraordinary. My second thought was to check that the call was genuine," he told Reuters in a telephone interview from his college rooms.
But he did not rank the prize as the greatest day of his life. He said that came in 1968 "when I finally cracked the optimal tax problem. It came in a flash and it was very satisfactory."

Mirrlees, who spent 27 years at Oxford University and is now Professor of Political Economy at Cambridge's Trinity College, has spent his life theorising on what is the optimium tax level that maintains a person's incentive to work.
Mirrlees, described by fellow economists as a self-effacing academic's academic, said: "It was really exciting solving a problem, a bit embarrassing to get a prize."

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said they were awarding Mirrlees and Vickrey the $1.12 million prize "for their fundamental contributions to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information".
The two men, who have not met, focussed on how governments, companies or any organisation could cope with constantly lacking complete information but having to make strategic decisions.
Mirrlees said he had concentrated on researching the links between levels of taxation and people's motivation to work.
He believes tax rates in Britain "could reasonably be higher, particularly for middle income earners."
Putting the average level of income tax and VAT (Value Added Tax) combined at less than 50 percent, he added: "I think it could well go above.
"It could become a disincentive but you could use the revenue for health services, education and welfare payments."
Economists singled out for praise the work that Mirrlees co-wrote in 1974 called "Project Appraisal and Planning."

"It became almost the bible for people looking to invest in developing countries," said Martin Weale, director of the National Institute For Economic and Social Research and one of the British treasury's panel of independent advisers.
He described Mirrlees as "a slightly austere Scotsman but an extraordinarily nice person."
"He's avoided macro forecasting so he's not as well known as some economists in this country but he is one of the country's leading economic theorists," he added.
